tagline.text: A Quezon City university museum tracing the roots of Philippine modern art

location.label: Location
location.text: Soledad V. Pangilinan Arts Wing, Areté, Ateneo de Manila University, Katipunan Avenue, Loyola Heights, Quezon City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (travel is easier in the dry season, November–May)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (per person, including admission, transport and snacks)

children.text: Built from works donated in 1960 by Fernando Zóbel, this is said to be the first university museum of Philippine modern and contemporary art. It now stages its exhibitions at Areté, the arts and innovation complex on the Ateneo campus.

The Ateneo Art Gallery is a university museum on the campus of Ateneo de Manila University in Loyola Heights, Quezon City. It is described as the first museum in the country devoted to Philippine modern art. It is not a noisy, crowded landmark like a big national museum; instead you can wander through a handful of galleries at an easy pace and get a clear picture of how Philippine modern art developed.
The story begins in

. Fernando Zóbel (1920–1984), a painter and art scholar who taught humanities and art appreciation at Ateneo, donated works by postwar Filipino artists as a study collection for students. The first donation is reported to have totaled 221 items: 67 paintings, 127 prints, 25 drawings and 2 sculptures. Later gifts from other donors and artists have grown the holdings to more than 500 works, including paintings, prints, drawings, sculptures, photographs and posters.
The gallery has changed homes several times. It started in Bellarmine Hall in 1961, moved to the ground floor of the Rizal Library in 1967, and then, around 2017–2018, moved into the
Soledad V. Pangilinan Arts Wing

of Areté, the new arts and innovation complex near the campus entrance. Sources disagree on whether the move happened in 2017 or 2018. The new building is reported to have seven or eight galleries and can display roughly 30% of the permanent collection at one time.

For travelers, the area around Intramuros and the National Museum in western Manila shows the Philippines of earlier eras, while this gallery shows what Filipino artists have painted since the mid-20th century. It pairs well with a stroll through the university district or a café stop in northeastern Quezon City as a half-day outing.

blocks.title: A collection that began with Zóbel's gift

children.text: The backbone of the museum is the set of works Fernando Zóbel donated between 1959 and 1964. The first work bought with the Zóbel Purchase Fund is reported to be Marciano Galang's "Cavite" (1964). You can see where Philippine modern art began, first-hand.

The collection includes early neorealist works by artists such as Hernando R. Ocampo, Vicente Manansala and Cesar Legaspi. You can follow the line from abstract expressionism through neorealism to later modernism in one visit.

blocks.title: Socially engaged art of the 1970s and 1980s

children.text: The gallery is also known for its strength in socially engaged (social realist) art of the 1970s and 1980s. In 2017 it staged "Ligalig," an exhibition of work from that period. The paintings let you read the mood of a society that lived through martial law.

blocks.title: Prints and drawings, from Rembrandt to Picasso

children.text: The collection holds more than 300 prints and drawings by local and international artists, from the Renaissance to the present. Rembrandt, Goya, Delacroix, Toulouse-Lautrec and Picasso are among the names mentioned. What is on view changes from time to time.
Running since 2004, the
Ateneo Art Awards

give the Fernando Zóbel Prizes in Visual Arts to young artists under 36. Winners receive grants for international residencies. Nominee exhibitions are held in the upper-floor galleries, so you can see where Philippine contemporary art is heading.

blocks.title: The first museum to collect video art

children.text: In 2011 the gallery became the first museum in the country to add video art to its permanent collection. The first video acquisitions include Kiri Dalena's "Erased Slogans" (2008). Depending on the exhibition, video works may be on view, so please keep your voice down.

blocks.title: Three permanent galleries and the exhibition galleries

children.text: Three ground-floor galleries rotate the permanent collection in themed shows. Five upper-floor galleries host short-term exhibitions. Among them are said to be the Wilson Sy Print and Drawing Gallery and a gallery named for the historian Ambeth Ocampo.

The same complex has a 900-seat theater and the roughly 250-seat Doreen Black Box Theater, along with an outdoor lawn between the buildings. On a performance day it is worth checking the schedule and combining a show with your museum visit.
Arrive on a weekday morning. The listed opening time is
, and many guides say it is open Monday to Saturday. Look for the Areté building beside Ateneo Gate 3 and enter the Arts Wing.

Check the admission information at the reception desk. Fees for outside visitors differ by source, so ask for the current rate on the spot. If you are asked to leave your bag, follow the instructions.
Start with the three permanent galleries on the ground floor. Take your time with early modern works by artists such as Ocampo and Manansala and the themed collection shows, and read the wall texts.
Go up to the special exhibition galleries on the upper floors. Shows change, so find out whether installations by contemporary artists, prints or drawings are on.
Finish with the outdoor space between the Areté buildings and the theater lobby. If there are performance posters, take a photo of the schedule.
Opening hours and closing days can change, so check the latest information by phone or email before you visit.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: The gallery and the university district

children.text: Get off at Katipunan Station on LRT-2 and walk along Katipunan Avenue, or take a jeepney or tricycle toward Ateneo. Map apps list the walk at about
17 minutes
Arrive at the Arts Wing and start with the ground-floor permanent galleries. Allow about 1–2 hours.
The area around Katipunan Avenue has many restaurants and cafés popular with students. Have a light lunch there.
If you have time, walk around the campus or the nearby university district. Follow the instructions on the day for entering the campus.
Take LRT-2 from Katipunan or call a ride-hailing car before rush hour. Katipunan Avenue is very congested in the morning and evening rush hours.
The easiest way from central Manila is LRT-2.
Katipunan Station
in Loyola Heights, Quezon City, is the closest rail station.
Katipunan is the only underground station on LRT-2. It opened in 2003, closed after a fire in 2019, and reopened on January 22, 2021.
From the station to the gallery (Areté) it is about
17 minutes
on foot according to map apps. If you would rather not walk, take a jeepney or tricycle.
Operating hours can change, so check LRTA announcements.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), you can take a taxi or ride-hailing car into the city and transfer to LRT-2. Travel time varies greatly with the time of day.

Tell the driver "Areté, next to Gate 3 of Ateneo de Manila University." Press coverage places Areté near Gate 3, across from Ricardo and Dr. Rosita Leong Hall, but the entry gate can change, so follow the booking instructions.
Katipunan Avenue is heavily congested at rush hour, so it is better to go right after the 9 a.m. opening or after lunch.
City bus routes, jeepneys and tricycles connect at Katipunan Station. Bus routes 3 and 7 are reported to stop at the Aurora–Katipunan interchange.
Routes and stops change often, so check a transit app or ask locals.
Areté is close to Gate 3, but the campus is large. Follow the instructions on the day for entering.
It is an indoor museum, so you can visit year-round. However, Quezon City gets a lot of rain in the wet season and traffic builds up easily, which can affect travel plans.

The gallery is reported to close on regular holidays and university holidays. The university calendar and exhibition changeovers may also affect it, so confirm it is open before you go. Ateneo Art Awards nominee shows and major special exhibitions vary by season.

The gallery itself has no accommodation. Northeastern Quezon City has university-district lodging and mid-range hotels along Katipunan Avenue, but most visitors stay a little farther south in Eastwood City or in central Manila and make this a day trip.

Restaurants, cafés and fast-food outlets popular with students cluster along Katipunan Avenue and the nearby streets. Shops change often, so check ratings and opening hours on the spot. The Areté complex has culinary school facilities, but whether it runs a regular restaurant has not been confirmed.

Before visiting, check opening hours and admission by email (aag@ateneo.edu) or phone (02-8426-6488). One source says it also opens on the first and third Sundays, but other sources do not mention this.
Going on a Monday-to-Saturday morning is likely to be quieter.
Only part of the collection is on view, so if you want to see a particular artist, check the current exhibition list before you go.
Wall texts may be mainly in English and Filipino. Have a translation app ready.
Rules on photography and flash may differ by exhibition, so follow the staff's instructions.
The Ateneo campus may have entry procedures, so bring an ID.
On performance days the Areté area may be crowded.
Opening hours and admission differ by source and cannot be confirmed. To avoid a wasted trip, always check the latest announcement before you go.
It closes on regular holidays and university holidays.
Katipunan Avenue is very congested at rush hour.
Roads can flood in the wet season, so check the weather and traffic information.
This is a university campus, so keep your voice down, do not run, and do not touch the artworks.
Keep your belongings close to you at all times.
A mixed-use district to the east of the gallery. It is a good place for meals and shopping, and by car it takes roughly
20–40 minutes
(depending on traffic).
The signature park of Quezon City, good for a walk. It is a drive from Ateneo, and the travel time varies greatly with traffic.
Heading east, you can visit the shoe museum and workshops in Marikina, which makes a good continuation of a cultural trip.
